The MQ-9 Reaper is a newer and upgraded version of the MQ-1 UAV.
The altitude of 5,000 m above sea level was chosen for the simulations, with an air pressure of 54,930 Pa.
The air density at 5,000 m altitude is 0.746 kg/m^3, and the dynamic viscosity is 1.63 x 10^-5 kg/(m*s).
The maximum speed of the MQ-9 Reaper is approximately 240 knots, or 123.467 m/s.
A high-order scheme with a 4th order difference and 3rd order time integral was used for the numerical scheme in the Flowsquare simulations.
The simulations were run for 5,000 time steps, with each time step lasting around 6.1138 x 10^-5 seconds.
The angles of attack simulated ranged from 0 to 20 degrees, in increments of 1 degree.
The critical angle of attack, where the airflow separates from the top surface of the wing, is around 16 degrees.
The NASA FoilSimJS software was used to approximate the lift and drag coefficients based on the airfoil parameters.
The lift coefficient steadily increased as the angle of attack increased, until the critical angle of attack was reached.
The drag coefficient also gradually increased as the angle of attack was increased.
The peak lift-to-drag ratio was found to be around 2 degrees angle of attack.
The Drela GW-19 airfoil is the root airfoil used in the MQ-9 Reaper.
UAVs like the MQ-9 Reaper can transmit data back to control stations about information such as altitude, aircraft speed, and target detection.
Intelligent UAVs can automatically respond to certain conditions, such as returning to the starting destination if they run out of fuel.
